Contentexpand_moreexpand_lessLearning objectives and content
    ObjectivesUnderstand and apply basic definitions and theorems from graph theory, concerning e.g. degree sequences, connectivity, bipartite graphs, trees, Euler graphs, Hamilton graphs, vertex and edge colorings, planarity, flows in directed graphs, matchings, vertex covers, edge covers, cliques and cocliques, adjacency matrices, graph isomorphism and automorphism groups.
Prove basic statements on graphs, and reason about (algorithmic) solutions to graph problems.
The student is aware of efficient standard algorithms for graph problems, is able to apply them, argue their correctness, and analyze their time complexity. Among these standard algorithms are Breadth-First Search, Depth-First Search, several shortest path algorithms and algorithms for finding a minimum weight spanning tree, a maximum flow in a directed graph, and a maximum cardinality (weight) matching in a bipartite graph.
Identify and devise models for problems that can be solved using graph concepts, theorems and algorithms covered in the course.
Apply the new graph theory knowledge and techniques to solve problems inspired by real-world challenges.
Design a (group) presentation concerning a graph model for a practical problem.
 

    ContentGraphs are mathematical objects especially suited to model all kinds of networks, but also many other practical situations can be described by a graph, a multigraph or a directed graph. In this course, which is primarily intended for applied mathematics students, graphs will be formally defined, studied, and analyzed with respect to several properties (such as connectedness, planarity, and chromatic number).  Special attention will be given to formally proving statements about graphs. Some connections between graph theory on the one hand, and set theory and (linear) algebra on the other hand, will be established. Moreover, several discrete optimization problems occurring in practice, like routing problems, scheduling problems and assignment problems, will be translated to graph problems. Efficient algorithms for several standard graph problems, like the shortest path problem, the maximum flow problem and the maximum matching problem, will be discussed and their efficiency will be analyzed. Finally, students will practice their modeling skills by translating well-defined problems inspired by real-world challenges to a graph setting,  and they will apply the knowledge obtained in the course by solving the corresponding graph problems or finding algorithmic solution methods.
